definition: A string of text that identifies your browser, operating system, and device to websites you visit, helping sites deliver compatible content but also enabling tracking.
metaDescription: Learn what a user agent is, how it identifies your browser and device to websites, and why it matters for your online privacy and security.
simpleExplanation: Think of your user agent as your browser's business card. Every time you visit a website, your browser automatically introduces itself by sharing details like "I'm Chrome on Windows" or "I'm Safari on iPhone." This helps websites show you the right version of their content.
whyItMatters: User agents can be used to track you across websites because your specific combination of browser, operating system, and device creates a unique fingerprint. This information helps build profiles of your browsing habits even without cookies.
technicalDetail: The User-Agent HTTP header contains structured information including browser name/version, rendering engine, operating system, and device type. Modern browsers send detailed strings like 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36' which can uniquely identify users when combined with other data points.

examples.explanation: When you visit a news site on your phone, the user agent tells the site you're using a mobile device, so it shows you the mobile-optimized version with larger buttons and simplified layout.
A streaming service checks your user agent to determine if your browser supports certain video formats, delivering the best quality stream your device can handle.
An advertising network uses your user agent along with other data like screen resolution and timezone to create a unique fingerprint, tracking your visits across multiple websites without cookies.
